item.title: Welcoming Sarah Cornejo ‘16 as Assistant Professor of Art
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Davidson’s art department is welcoming back alum Sarah Elizabeth Cornejo ’16 as their newest faculty member: Assistant Professor of Art in Sculpture and Drawing. As an undergraduate student at Davidson, Cornejo earned her B.A. in Studio Art and English Literature. Since graduating, she has lived in New Orleans and Memphis, completing various residencies and fellowships...
item.content:encoded:
Davidson’s art department is welcoming back alum Sarah Elizabeth Cornejo ’16 as their newest faculty member: Assistant Professor of Art in Sculpture and Drawing. 

As an undergraduate student at Davidson, Cornejo earned her B.A. in Studio Art and English Literature. Since graduating, she has lived in New Orleans and Memphis, completing various residencies and fellowships and earning her M.F.A at UNC Chapel Hill in hopes of teaching. 

Cornejo replaces Cort Savage, a former Professor of Art, following his retirement. After a rigorous national and international search led by Associate Professor of Art Tyler Starr to fill the tenure-track position, Cornejo was selected from among finalists.

Cornejo has previously taught at Davidson as a visiting faculty member, and art department chair, John Corso-Esquivel stated that Cornejo stood out because of her advanced technical skills, including welding, bronze casting, and woodworking and her unique literary approach to art.

“[Her work] is both carefully researched and meticulously crafted. Professor Cornejo brings an approach that is especially valuable at Davidson: a love of reading and theoretical inquiry combined with a deep dedication to studio craft,” Corso-Esquivel explained in an email to The Davidsonian. 

Cornejo’s work explores themes of hybridity, disrupting binaries, ambiguity, and existing in undefined spaces through sculpture. Her Peruvian heritage inspires her to focus on the serpents of Latin American mythology. Expanding beyond traditional mediums, she uses found objects, such as shells from the beaches of North Carolina or used bullet cases, to convey the elusiveness of these serpents, who are said to dwell in deep waters and caves.

The theoretical side of her work is complemented by her technical skill. “She brings together the well-read Davidson approach with a deep love of experimentation in the studio,” said Corso-Esquivel. 

Cornejo credits part of her career success to Davidson, which gave her a strong work ethic. Her double major in English Literature and Studio Art gave her important experience in conducting research and creating work that actively engages in and responds to real-time conversations.

“Davidson was the best preparation I’ve had of anything I’ve done since then for just how to think critically, how to think about why what you’re learning matters in a real way… every professor I had was just amazing and really cared… they cared about me [and] they cared about what they were teaching. They cared about the world, and that’s really inspiring to be around.”

Notably, Cornejo is a 2025–2030 Joan Mitchell Fellow, a national-level fellowship that awards each fellow $60,000 in unrestricted funds as well as personalized networking opportunities and peer engagement over a five-year period.

One of Cornejo’s personal highlights so far has been meeting and working with new students and colleagues. “[It’s] a privilege to be back. I have really great students this semester, which feels like such a gift […] So I think people [have] been a highlight.”

Students feel similarly. Cornejo is already making waves on campus and inspiring students such as Bella Rosenfeld ’27. 

“I really like that she’s a Davidson grad. I always just love professors who have been educated here, especially when you’re in the art department…it’s really impactful to be taught by somebody who made a career out of the arts at this [very] school…it’s nice to know that she’s been in my position, she’s been in my role.”

Returning to Davidson as an educator rather than a student provides Cornejo with familiarity of Davidson as an institution. However, she acknowledges that a lot has changed since her time as a student, and she is interested in seeing how students’ interests have changed and how to best support them as a professor. 

“Being in this role [of a professor] versus being in a student role is, of course, very different. So I’m curious to see what students are interested in learning now, what processes they’re interested in now, and being responsive to that.”

Cornejo is not the only Davidson alum in the art department. She joins Lyla Halsted ’14, Assistant Professor of Art in the art history department. Rosenfeld shares her excitement to have Davidson alumni in both realms of the art department: “It’s an exciting opportunity to now have a Davidson alum in both the art history department and the studio art department, and to kind of have that impact in both senses of the word ‘art’. I think it can be very powerful, and there’s a lot of potential there.” 

Corso-Esquivel echoes Rosenfeld’s sentiments. “As a Davidson graduate, Professor Cornejo understands firsthand the distinctive character of a liberal arts education here. Her return adds a faculty member who can connect serious intellectual inquiry with ambitious studio experimentation,” he said. “That combination will benefit both art majors and students encountering studio art for the first time.”

Cornejo turns to reading and poetry to find inspiration for her work, but she also feels that teaching will complement her work and bolster her creativity: “I really feel like teaching and my work go well together. Things get too intense one way or the other without both.”

item.title: Elizabeth Wellington Rollins ‘10 Returns with Debut Novel
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Following the release of her USA Today bestseller debut, The Three Graces of Pearl Street, Elizabeth Wellington Rollins ’10, returned to campus for a book signing at Main Street Books this past Saturday. The novel is based on a Roman myth of the Three Graces, minor goddesses who each personify a feminine virtue. Rollins channels...
item.content:encoded:
Following the release of her USA Today bestseller debut, The Three Graces of Pearl Street, Elizabeth Wellington Rollins ’10, returned to campus for a book signing at Main Street Books this past Saturday. 

The novel is based on a Roman myth of the Three Graces, minor goddesses who each personify a feminine virtue. Rollins channels them through three intergenerational protagonists: ninety-six-year-old grandmother Graziella, her daughter Grace, and her granddaughter Ella. In an interview with the Davidsonian, Rollins described the plot through the grandmother: “Graziella rules her family, her neighborhood, her parish church’s food kitchen, a feral cat program, all with an iron fist and arms full of lasagna and chicken cutlets.” 

The event was moderated by Davidson professor Chris Marsicano ’10, an old friend of Rollins from her time as a Davidson student. Rollins spoke fondly of her time at Davidson.. “It’s absolutely delightful to be back.” She said, reflecting on seeing Marsicano during her weekend on campus., “I got to see him and his wife and daughter this morning. His wife is also in the class of 2010 and was in the same freshman hall as me.” 

Rollins credited her Davidson education with shaping her novel. “I think that [the diverse topics mentioned in her novel] are things that I was able to weave together because of the interdisciplinary aspects and nature of my education here.”

Furthering her Davidson connections, Rollins hired a current Davidson student, Julia Carey ’27, as her marketing intern. Carey finds working for an alum fulfilling and eye-opening. “It’s been a great opportunity to further develop my social media skills and gain insight into the world of publishing,” she said. “I’ve been inspired by the way [Rollins’] Davidson experience has influenced her writing career.” 

Attendees were also treated to a special touch: a mini magazine filled with six recipes, one placed on every chair at the event. Rollins explained that they were reserved for attendees of her book tour and those who pre-ordered the book.  

The recipes come straight from Rollins’ family kitchen. “My great-uncle and aunt ran an Italian market in a New York neighborhood where this book takes place. It was called Fava’s. And, my uncle Tony Fava married a woman named Toni. So they became Tony and Toni Fava,” Rollins said, smiling. “I got my family’s blessing to include some recipes in a little packet with the book.” 

Rollins revealed that her family inspired more than just the recipes. “My only Italian and Italian-American heritage is through my grandmother, Lucia, and so to me it was a matriarchy because I was raised by her, my mom, and my grandmother’s four sisters.” That matriarchy is evident on the back of the recipe magazines, where Rollins shares family traditions alongside an old photo of the women smiling among friends, inviting readers into her private world.

Rollins wrote an article for People magazine describing how she wanted to depict Italian-American culture differently than other popular culture media such as The Godfather and The Sopranos, which spotlight Italian American men in dangerous, morally grey situations. “I wanted to write a novel [about women doing great things] that gave as much layers and depth and was as engaging […] as one could be about men doing awful things,” Rollins noted during the event.

According to Rollins, the novel’s conflict is personal and centers on how people love each other differently across generations. “I wanted to read about three generations of women who all have those values, but have completely different points of view on how to bring them into the world effectively,” she said.

Main Street Books owner Adah Fitzgerald ‘01, who has owned the store since 2015, spoke to how many authors come to Davidson for events. “We host a lot of Davidson alumni because a lot of them are great writers. It’s an ebb and flow of receiving event pitches from other people, either from publicists or authors themselves […] And sometimes we do outreach.” 

The front table of the cozy bookstore was filled with books signed by bestselling authors. Fitzgerald advised students interested in future Main Street books events to visit the store’s online website and Instagram page.

Reflecting on the novel’s success , Rollins expressed excitement about the book’s rollout. “We’ve sold six foreign rights in six languages, and so there are editors in Serbia, Germany, Poland, and the Netherlands.” 

Rollins is an atmospheric author who strives to capture a specific moment, feeling, and journey for  her characters. “This book feels like home […] and so whenever I feel despair about the state of the world, you know, you kind of remember that there’s a universality in the specificity.”

item.title: Davidson Athletics signs with Nike after Under Armour split
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: After a 10-year partnership with Under Armour, Davidson College athletics has repartnered with Nike. The college announced the new partnership on June 10. Under the agreement, BSN Sports will exclusively supply Nike uniforms, apparel, footwear, accessories and equipment to all 21 of Davidson’s varsity teams. Davidson’s partnership with Under Armour came to a close on...
item.content:encoded:
After a 10-year partnership with Under Armour, Davidson College athletics has repartnered with Nike.

The college announced the new partnership on June 10. Under the agreement, BSN Sports will exclusively supply Nike uniforms, apparel, footwear, accessories and equipment to all 21 of Davidson’s varsity teams.

Davidson’s partnership with Under Armour came to a close on July 1. Davidson Vice President and Director of Athletics Chris Clunie ’06 explained that the decision was due partially to Davidson basketball alumnus Stephen Curry: the Golden State Warrior star departed from Under Armour in 2025 and joined Chinese sportswear company Li-Ning in June.

“We were lockstep with Stephen [Curry],” Clunie said. “If he would have stayed with Under Armour, we would have stayed.”

When Davidson signed with Under Armour in 2016, Under Armour described Davidson as an important part of its story because it was the alma mater of one of the company’s most prominent athletes—Curry. Initially, men’s basketball remained sponsored by Nike, but followed suit with the rest of Davidson athletics donning Under Armour apparel two years later.

Although Davidson College and Curry are no longer under contract with the same sportswear brand, Clunie emphasized that the relationship between the college and its most recognizable alum remains strong as ever.

“We are with Nike, but we are always going to be part of ‘Team Stephen,’” Clunie said. “We’re going to continue to work and support his new endeavor and Curry Brand in pretty innovative and creative ways in the future.”

Davidson men’s basketball head coach Matt McKillop believes the student-athletes felt strongly toward their ties with Curry Brand as well. “I thought there was a great appreciation for that, there was a great sense of pride,” he said.

After Curry signed with Li Ning, Davidson looked for a brand capable of serving the entire athletic department. “Li Ning is really focused on basketball, and it opened up the opportunity for us to look at a partnership [with a different brand] for all of Davidson Athletics,” Clunie said. 

Field hockey player Elyse Unger ’27 said athletes began thinking about what would come next for the college after Curry left Under Armour.

“I think a lot of athletes had an idea that something new was coming,” Unger said.

Unger described the reaction among current and prospective athletes. “I don’t know if people are actually going to make their recruitment decisions based on a logo, but it definitely is a plus,” Unger said. “I’d say the freshmen coming in are very excited about the change.”

Women’s basketball player Eliza Buerk ’27 is looking forward to being a Nike-sponsored college athlete.

“I wore Nike shoes and Nike gear all throughout high school, and I have a bunch of Nike shoes that I got to bring back to school with me that I’m excited to start wearing again,” she said. 

For Buerk, the brand change represents something bigger. “I’m excited to wear shoes that were designed by women with the Sabrinas and the A’ja Wilsons,” she explained. “That’s a pretty unique opportunity that not a lot of companies currently offer.”

Although many are excited about the new Nike era, McKillop does not expect the partnership to play a major role in recruiting.

“I don’t think anybody’s going to come to Davidson or not come to Davidson because of a shoe company,” McKillop said. “I think Davidson, the values we have at the school, the academics, the environment here, I think people are going to make decisions more for that than what shoe brand we have.”

The transition is not happening instantly, as many fall sports teams ordered uniforms as early as December 2025 for this year’s season, months before the Nike partnership was announced leading to many teams having to cover logos on existing uniforms until replacements arrive.

Cross country runner Graham Boles ’29 feels the impact of the brand change. “Because of Curry, we were higher up on the priority list with Under Armour,” Boles said. “There are so many Nike schools that we are now just one of many.”

The partnership is a return to the same brand Davidson’s athletic leaders played under during their time at Davidson. Clunie and McKillop both played men’s basketball at Davidson from 2002 to 2006, when the Wildcats wore Nike.

“When we made the Elite Eight in 2008 Nike did some special things for us,” said McKillop. He remembers his Nike “Witness” shirt to commemorate Davidson’s historical run. Curry led Davidson past Gonzaga, Georgetown and Wisconsin before the Wildcats lost by two points to eventual national champion Kansas.

McKillop believes this rebranding will draw positive attention to Davidson’s basketball program. “[With the brand] I think a lot of people think of great basketball players, many of them are aligned with Nike,” he said. “Chris Clunie worked very, very hard to make sure we had something to be very excited about.”

item.title: Soccer continues undefeated season in A10 opener
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Davidson Men’s Soccer broke through for their first win of the season on Friday, defeating George Mason University 3-2. The ’Cats (1-0-4) keep their undefeated record intact and begin Atlantic 10 play with a win. Enthusiasm for a strong early season comes through in overwhelming support from their classmates in Davidson’s growing student section, “The...
item.content:encoded:
Davidson Men’s Soccer broke through for their first win of the season on Friday, defeating George Mason University 3-2. The ’Cats (1-0-4) keep their undefeated record intact and begin Atlantic 10 play with a win. Enthusiasm for a strong early season comes through in overwhelming support from their classmates in Davidson’s growing student section, “The Pack.”

George Mason had been marked on the team’s schedule since June as one of great importance, not only because it was the first A10 game of the season but also to avenge last season’s playoff loss to the Patriots. “You’re going to have two very hungry teams that are very different in identity, and come out and see who can get three points,” Wildcats head coach Mike Babst said before the matchup.

Davidson got off to a hot start with Nico Zeballos ’29 scoring an early goal in the match’s 14th minute. After George Mason equalized, Myles Culley ’27, the team’s lead scorer last season, got Davidson the lead back with a header in the 41st minute. George Mason was once again able to claw their way back into the game with a strike early in the second half.

For a moment it looked like the team would continue the streak of ties until Pablo Linzoain ’29 netted the game winner in the 65th minute, keeping the undefeated streak alive while also securing the team’s first win of the season.

With this win, the ’Cats hope to continue carrying the momentum through the rest of the season. “Getting that first win kind of kickstarts things,” Matthew Thissell ’27 said. “If we win that game then we find a rhythm of winning games.”

The victory came in the face of strong adversity as the ’Cats have had to navigate some unfortunate injuries. Team captain and defensive leader Nico Quanbeck ’27 went down with a torn ACL just before the season started.

Before the game, Thissell emphasized the importance of keeping the team’s morale and focus in check.  “I think the biggest thing from a leadership standpoint is making sure everyone still has that belief and that drive, and that they understand that we’re able to get results even with a couple key guys out,” Thissell said.

Babst’s squad is no stranger to adversity. Last season Davidson went from not winning a game in the month of September to finishing fourth in the Atlantic 10 conference and making it all the way to the conference tournament semi-finals. This sense of resilience is just as strong this year, and there is no doubt amongst the team as to what they are capable of. 

The ’Cats return most of their key veterans from last season, a seasoned group relied upon to provide leadership and guidance to younger players who have had to step into larger roles in place of injured teammates.

Friday’s performance capped off a very unusual start to the season, which saw the team tying their first four games, two of which were against nationally ranked opponents.

Davidson opened with a 1-1 draw against Charlston, who played a man down for the final 7 minutes after a player received two yellows. They proceeded to draw two draws in their next three games against Gardner-Webb, #14 UNC Greensboro, and #21 Furman.

Solid performances from the ’Cats against ranked teams were a source of encouragement early in the season. “The last two games showed that we’re a hard team to beat, and we can compete with some of the best teams in the country,” said midfielder Brady McGlone ’28 before the match.

This year, thanks to the efforts of student leaders James Buford ’29, Will Lowance ’27, and Gabriel Onoratini ’29, the student section has been packed every gameday. As put by Buford, their goal is to “reach all corners of the school,” and unify the community around the soccer team to create an electrifying atmosphere at Alumni Stadium.

These efforts have not only been appreciated by students, who have been showing out for home games this year, but by players and coaches as well.

“Teams are coming here and feeling like this is one of the best atmospheres in college soccer, which is pretty awesome,” Babst said.

As “The Pack” continues to grow, the support will only get stronger as the season goes on. “We’re all close with the soccer guys,” Onoratini said. “When we receive a message from one of the players after the game thanking us for our support, that just makes us want to continue more.”

The season thus far has been indicative of what a strong community and supporting cast can do, even in times of uncertainty. The support from fans and amongst the players themselves have rallied the team together and, so far, have delivered promising results. 

It’s clear that the ’Cats have something special this year. “There’s a real kind of confidence and spirit to this group,” Babst said. “There’s just a ton of potential for what they can do.”

As momentum continues to build throughout the season, the support will continue to build amongst those who show out at Alumni Stadium every home game.

The ’Cats will defend their undefeated record at home for the next three matches; Davidson hosts High Point University on Tuesday, Elon University on Sep. 22, and resumes conference play against St. Bonaventure University on Sep. 26.

item.title: Living here and there
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: I live two lives here at Davidson College. Not the Spider-Man and Peter Parker kind of double life. My second life here at Davidson is exactly nine hours behind my first in Islamabad, Pakistan. Going into my third week of classes as a first-year, I have been debating which life actually deserves to be put...
item.content:encoded:
I  live two lives here at Davidson College. Not the Spider-Man and Peter Parker kind of double life. My second life here at Davidson is exactly nine hours behind my first in Islamabad, Pakistan. 

Going into my third week of classes as a first-year, I have been debating which life actually deserves to be put first. 

You see, my first life was technically my only life until I decided to move across the globe for college. Before moving to North Carolina, the phrase “don’t forget where you come from” sounded vaguely dystopian to me. Remembering home was simple enough. How could I forget it?

“My name is Sarah Shahzad. I’m a freshman from Pakistan.” 

“Yes, I’m used to the heat back home, it’s pretty similar.” 

“Yeah, my hometown has lots of trails around, too.”

As I am sure other freshmen can relate, during the first couple of weeks of college I found myself frequently repeating these answers to commonly asked questions.

But remembering home was never supposed to be reduced to the weather and the trees. I was suddenly confronted with the need to squeeze in ten-minute calls between classes in an attempt to feel the comforts of home. I gave fragmented rundowns of my day to parents who attentively listened to tasks they didn’t understand while they told me about stories that had already happened, stories I was meant to experience first-hand. 

“Make sure you’re keeping subjects that have market value in the future,” my dad encouraged me on one call.

“Yes, Baba, I will do that, but we have a lot of time to explore a variety of different subjects before deciding.”

My surprised question, “Omg! When did you rearrange my room?” received my mother’s equally offhand response: “It has actually been a while now. Your brother wanted to have more open space in the room.”

I feel the sense of familiarity that the mention of home brings fading away as I no longer know which new decoration piece has been added to my mother’s overflowing collection or which new joke has begun to dominate the dinner space. Evenings aren’t welcomed anymore with large pots of tea and an array of assorted biscuits. I no longer know whether the ice cream man has my favourite flavor today. While orienting myself to the new faces here, I find myself reorienting, concerned I’ll end up forgetting those over a thousand miles away. 

Coming to Davidson, I didn’t realize that I wouldn’t just have to adjust to the college experience – I would also have to readjust the life that had always been there. In these few short weeks, my experience of home has changed from knowing the exact positions of all the cracks in the walls to being in the periphery. Davidson seemingly takes center stage in my camera roll and discussions, while the peripheral life resides alongside it. 

Jokes that can never be translated into English live alongside the new traditions here that never existed back home. Within those ten-minute calls, I catch up on the family drama, courtesy of my mother’s expert storytelling skills, before going back to planning out costume options for Halloween with my friends for the first time (apparently planning two months in advance is not that early). 

This isn’t a piece on how I blended my two lives but rather it is an acceptance of the fact that these two lives are distinct in nature and that they aren’t meant to be numbered in terms of importance. My host parent hangs a Pakistani flag on her house while she introduces me to the most quintessentially American things like making s’mores over a bonfire. Pieces of my old life come through people I meet at Davidson who are able to recognize and make space for that life without having been a part of it. 

With four years still ahead of me, I am excited to see the different ways these lives evolve and what new roles I take up in both of them. Even if the dream of having my high school best friend come visit me in college might remain a dream, I’ll continue to recognize pieces of her in the friends I make here. I stand within the circle of the nine-hour gap, not behind or ahead, but rather in just the right place to be able to watch the cricket team lose in the afternoon and have Cookout in the parking lot at night. 

Sarah Shahzad is undecided from Islamabad, Pakistan and can be reached for comment at contact@example.edu.

item.title: In defense of Kirkification: open debate is a myth
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Charlie Kirk built a career convincing college students that “free speech” meant an obligation to platform whoever asked for it, and that “civil discourse” meant handing a microphone to an inexperienced 19-year-old and calling it a debate. It was a theater designed to create clips of “owning the libs.” He made a mockery of the...
item.content:encoded:
Charlie Kirk built a career convincing college students that “free speech” meant an obligation to platform whoever asked for it, and that “civil discourse” meant handing a microphone to an inexperienced 19-year-old and calling it a debate. It was a theater designed to create clips of “owning the libs.” He made a mockery of the unpracticed debater as a way to “prove” he was correct. A waste of air. This forum put a veil over his bigoted views and framed them as simply an engagement with free expression. 

I don’t believe we have an obligation to engage with these ideas; in doing so, we only validate them as worthy of engagement. Debate is not simply a free expression of ideas, it’s a mechanism for building power.

One of last week’s Perspectives pieces reflected on a YikYak mockery of Kirk and Davidson’s TPUSA Chapter. From my understanding, the writer took the YikYak comment as representative of the idea that Davidson students have lost the appetite for genuine disagreement – that mockery has replaced argument. I disagree. I think the post is evidence that many students feel there is no value in engaging with bigots. 

I agree with this writer’s point that doing victory laps over Kirk’s death isn’t pragmatic. Gloating isn’t a strategy for success and won’t change anyone’s mind. But there’s a difference between gloating over a political win and refusing to dignify an ideology of hate with a debate it doesn’t deserve.

Creating a norm in political discourse where the only acceptable response to hateful rhetoric is calm, critical engagement is both unrealistic and bad faith. There’s no obligation to spend your energy on neutral engagement with an idea or organization whose function is to push white nationalist rhetoric. 

Perhaps this non-platforming approach is too little too late. Kirk and his bigoted ideology have already been platformed; many ideals are reflected by the current White House administration. Refusing to engage with the TPUSA chapter on campus doesn’t undo this crawl to power. But it does prevent adding fuel to the fire.

This is why I find mockery of Charlie Kirk and the Kirkification meme both funny and pragmatic. Kirkification successfully de-martyred Charlie Kirk. People were fired from their jobs over negative comments on Charlie Kirk’s legacy. Where was the freedom of expression for the people losing their jobs over a joke? The right successfully pressured employers to treat criticism of a MAGA icon with the same severity as hate speech.

But Kirkification prevented, or more accurately stalled, a crackdown on anti-Trumpism dissent. MAGA is already willing to label loosely defined left-wing movements like Antifa as domestic terrorists. If Kirk’s death was given the seriousness the right wanted, I don’t doubt they would have used it as a tool for broader suppression. It’s hard for the right to treat his death as a call to arms when people associate his memory with the image of his face superimposed onto iShowSpeed. 

To summarize a line by Mel Brooks explaining why he turned Hitler into a punchline in “The Producers”: you can’t beat an orator on a soapbox with another speech, but you can make him look ridiculous, and that’s a real kind of victory. 

I don’t think Davidson’s TPUSA chapter should be kicked off campus. I do believe in free expression. But I also reserve the right to react to that expression. Treating “free expression” as a neutral, consequence-free zone is insular. Say something racist, and people are going to react with contempt, mockery or otherwise. That mockery isn’t a violation of anyone’s expression. It’s what free expression actually looks like when more than one person is using it. 

My qualms regarding the push to engage with bigoted viewpoints stretches beyond the TPUSA chapter at Davidson to the administration’s discussion of “bridging political gaps.”

Bridge-building rhetoric assumes that if we all just talk more respectfully, incrementalism will get us somewhere – but incrementalism is failing. Extremism doesn’t purely come from failures to productively disagree; extremism is a child of extreme situations: immense inflation, impossible healthcare and housing costs, imminent climate change disasters. Kirk’s rhetoric promoting culture wars is incompatible with genuine systematic critiques. But both are reactions to the same impossible situation young people find themselves in. Time spent “building consensus” is time the actual conditions generating the anger grow. 

Civility is not the problem, but treating it as the solution is. 

Mockery and refusal to engage are not failures in civic formality, but tools for engaging an increasingly entertainment-focused political world. Dialogue is worth pursuing, but slow by design. Urgent problems need tangible solutions.

Jonah Feld is a Public Health major from Lexington, KY. He can be reached for comment at contact@example.edu.

item.title: “Divine Nine” participation increases
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: The National Pan-Hellenic Council comprises nine historically Black Greek-letter organizations, each rooted in service, leadership, and community. At Davidson over the past year, the NPHC has witnessed a significant increase in membership. Davidson currently has four active chapters, including two fraternities, Alpha Phi Alpha Inc. and Kappa Alpha Psi Inc., and two sororities, Alpha Kappa...
item.content:encoded:
The National Pan-Hellenic Council comprises nine historically Black Greek-letter organizations, each rooted in service, leadership, and community. At Davidson over the past year, the NPHC has witnessed a significant increase in membership. 

Davidson currently has four active chapters, including two fraternities, Alpha Phi Alpha Inc. and  Kappa Alpha Psi Inc., and two sororities, Alpha Kappa Alpha Inc. and Delta Sigma Theta Inc. They provide students opportunities to find community, develop meaningful connections, and engage in service both on and beyond Davidson’s campus. 

While each organization has its own traditions and history, together they contribute to the growing presence of the Divine Nine at Davidson.

“After last spring, I believe there were almost 30 of us, and I personally think that that’s the largest NPHC council that I’ve seen or I’ve heard about from years past,” said Zariah Johnson ’28, president of the Upsilon Mu chapter of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Incorporated. 

Davidson’s chapter of Alpha Phi Alpha, a one-person chapter last year, jumped to six members over the past year. 

After spending two years as the chapter’s sole member, Jamal Chandler-Fuller’s ’27 experience shifted when five new members joined, allowing him to share the responsibilities of maintaining and growing the chapter.

“It was like a dream come true. That was, that was one of my, my proudest days,” Chandler said. “It was nerve-wracking for sure. Just trying to make sure that I taught them everything that I learned and that they were well equipped because I knew what that was like when I was coming in.” 

For president of the Sigma Psi chapter of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Incorporated, Megan Banks ’28, growth also means more than numbers. “Part of growth to me means we are doing more community service as a whole with all four organizations,” she said. “Even though we are all a part of different organizations and we kind of all have our different mottos and different purposes, we all are a united front, and we are all here to serve the Davidson community and beyond.” 

The solidarity within NPHC holds special significance at Davidson, which is a predominantly White institution. According to College Tuition Compare data from the 24-25 academic year, 6.8% of the student body is Black. 

For NPHC members, finding community within their chapter at a predominantly White institution provides crucial safe places and support for Black students. NPHC is a physically present force on campus, consistently hosting events, performing service, and collaborating with other organizations. 

These events provide opportunities for NPHC chapters to connect with the broader Davidson community while creating spaces for students to engage with their work. Recently, Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Incorporated, in partnership with Black Femmes of Davidson, hosted a focused panel discussion on navigating a predominantly white institution. Johnson herself attended the event to support and participate.

For Johnson, the growth of the NPHC is reflected not only in membership numbers, but also in increased collaboration and support between chapters.  “And it’s not forced. Like, a lot of us are friends outside of the letters and outside of NPHC… being able to show that we are united as one is one of my biggest things, to be able to show people that NPHC is a strong community and that we’re not going to back down if anything happens.” 

The NPHC council represents more than Greek letters or strolling. It allows members to bring different perspectives and experiences into the larger campus community. 

 “This is not something I joined just so I could wear Greek letters. I didn’t join it so I could do a certain type of dance,” member of the Davidson’s chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and captain of the football team, Christian Lyons ‘28, remarked. “I joined it because I wanted to make an impact. And this organization and this group of people, I feel like it represents the things that I want to do and I want to be known for.” 

Members hope to build something sustainable that continues to flourish after its current leaders graduate. “Our history and impact are something the entire Davidson community can learn from and appreciate,” Collins said. “More education and support would help NPHC continue to grow and build stronger, more sustainable chapters on campus.”

item.title: AI is expanding — so is the Honor Council
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Two years ago the Honor Council adjudicated 12 student violation cases. Last year, there were 60. 80% of Honor Council cases from last year were AI-related Honor Code violations, according to Associate Dean of Students Shawn McQuillan-Krepps. Across college campuses, AI and questions of its ethical use, are running rampant. Research from the Lumina Foundation-Gallup...
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago the Honor Council adjudicated 12 student violation cases. Last year, there were 60. 

80% of Honor Council cases from last year were AI-related Honor Code violations, according to Associate Dean of Students Shawn McQuillan-Krepps. Across college campuses, AI and questions of its ethical use, are running rampant. Research from the Lumina Foundation-Gallup 2026 State of Higher Education study shows that 57% of college students use AI at least weekly. 

The large influx of cases has been the topic of many conversations on campus between students and staff alike. 

Dean of Faculty Shelley Rigger blames the increase in part on AI. “I think the increase in cases is partly due to AI, which has, one, made cheating more tempting and two, made it harder for some students to recognize when they are violating the Honor Code,” she said. 

AI has caused considerable panic among faculty and Davidson College leadership. Many professors have declared their classes “tech-free” environments and have transitioned to only in-person or oral exams.

Rigger acknowledged that many students believe there is an increase in exam center testing instead of take-home tests, but said the shift is not as drastic as students think. “Take-home exams have not always been common; for most of the time I’ve been here, most faculty gave their exams in the Exam Center. Just as an example, in spring 2010, there were 2,658 exams given in the Exam Center, compared to 1,450 in spring 2026.” 

While AI is largely the leading cause of Honor Code violations, multiple other factors are contributing to the four-time increase in student adjudication. 

One is that professors are reporting at higher rates. “Faculty are reporting cases, in part because they know that the only way to stop AI cheating is to let students know that we aren’t going to look the other way,” said Rigger. 

Professors have been reluctant in past years to report cheating to the Honor Council due to lengthy case processing times. 

“I do think the process for faculty can sometimes be cumbersome because they have to refer students to the Honor Council, and then it’s a process that takes time,” Dean of Students Marquita Barker said. 

This year, however, the Honor Council has significantly improved their efficiency.  

“The thing we want faculty to remember is that if you suspect an Honor Code violation in your class, you really need to refer it to the Honor Council and not try to adjudicate it in your classroom,” Barker said. 

Silas Garrett ’27, an Honor Council student solicitor, is part of the honor council’s efforts to increase efficiency on the council. “We’ve been able to process cases much more efficiently, and I think we’ve also emphasized faculty buy-in.” 

In order to do this, the Honor Council has implemented more leadership roles, increasing from one pair of student solicitors and student defense advisors to two pairs of each.

Charlotte Frampton ’27, the vice chair of the Honor Council, highlighted positive results.“They split the [case loads], which has been super helpful for them because three years ago, student solicitors and defense advisors were super overwhelmed, and so we are adapting to having so many more cases by literally changing our procedures,” she said. 

The Council has also been working to build trust with faculty members. In years past, the Honor Council and faculty have not always seen eye-to-eye. 

“When I got to the honor council, there was a really big tension between the honor council and the faculty and the administration. They did not like each other,” Frampton said. “There’s been a really big effort from the faculty and the administration, and also from the students on the honor council, to repair that relationship and to rebuild the trust between the honor council and the students and the faculty.”

Council members have also been working closely with the D.G. and Harriet Wall Martin Institute for Public Good, in another effort to improve relationships and transparency between the Council and faculty.  

“They’re [students] meeting with Event Contact from the Martin Institute in terms of an ethics program, ethics on their leadership,” said McQuillan-Krepps. “They meet directly with the vice president for academic affairs and dean of faculty, Dr. Shelley Rigger. They do some faculty panels, hear from faculty what their perspectives are.”

Working with the faculty has led to positive results, including the growth of “mutual resolution,” a process implemented in the spring semester of 2024 as an alternative to a trial.  

McQuillan-Krepps described mutual resolution as, “the idea that the student is saying ‘I did it, I cheated, I don’t want to deny it.’ The professor saying, ‘They did it, they cheated, can we just work and come to a resolution together in partnership with the Honor Council.’”

Mutual resolution is contingent on the student having no prior Honor Code violations. It entails a meeting with the Honor Council, the professor who reported the violation and the student. The final resolution is agreed upon by all parties. 

Frampton believes the council needs to increase transparency with students. “Something that the Honor Council needs to work on, which is something I’m trying to work on, is just more outreach to the student body, more visibility,” she said. “Making sure that the student body knows what’s happening, and it’s not like a secret process.”

Students at Davidson College tend to lack knowledge about the Honor Council because of the confidential nature of the council and their proceedings.

“It needs to be thought of less as a shadowy group that’s lurking behind a corner waiting to catch you, and more of just a group of students who I think everyone here, are completely involved in trying to make impunity as good as it can be,” said Brooks Pinney ’27, an Honor Council student solicitor.

While procedural aspects of the Honor Council are changing, the Honor Code itself is not. The Honor Code is integral to the fabric of Davidson College, and it has remained ingrained in the community.

“The Honor Code is not just about doing your own homework and not cheating on tests. It’s about learning to turn your back on a dishonest shortcut. It’s about becoming a trustworthy individual that others look to for leadership and inspiration,” said Rigger. 

“Smart people go here, nice people go here, and that’s all true, but it’s the honor code that really makes that binding between students,” Pinney said.

item.title: 900 room bar closes to student-run events
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: As Davidson student activities kick off and live Thursday performances reverberate around the Student Union, a major change has become evident: the 900 Room Bar is no longer operating during student events. During previous years, the bar in the 900 Room would serve beer on tap while student events were held in the room, most...
item.content:encoded:
As Davidson student activities kick off and live Thursday performances reverberate around the Student Union, a major change has become evident: the 900 Room Bar is no longer operating during student events. 

During previous years, the bar in the 900 Room would serve beer on tap while student events were held in the room, most notably during Live Thursday. Now, while the bar is not closed completely, it is no longer staffed by student bartenders and is only open to student-run programming by request. The bar is only open during non-student events and staffed by bartenders from Much Ado, Davidson’s catering company. 

The bar was opened in 2001 along with the Student Union to serve 21+ students and adult community members during events – both student-led and not. 

According to Emily Eisenstadt, director of the College Union, the bar’s closing was purely a financial decision. “This wasn’t a one year quick decision but steadily the bar was losing money,” said Eisenstadt. “There was rarely a night when we were breaking even.”

 The Student Union even attempted to keep the bar open by raising beer prices by $2 last year. However, according to Eisenstadt, this proved ineffective. “Then we saw even less people wanting to purchase,” she said. “So we felt [we] were out of options.” 

Though this decision comes in the wake of enforcement of stronger alcohol rules at Davidson, the Union Board Director assures that the bar’s closing is solely financial. “We would be totally fine if there are events that have alcohol in the 900 Room,” said Eisenstadt. “We just want it managed well by licensed bartenders.” 

This means that if a student organization wants to host an event in the 900 Room with alcohol, they are permitted to request use of the bar so long as it is operated by bartenders from Much Ado instead of by students. 

Eisenstadt notes that bartending at the 900 Room bar was an aspect of a job these students were already doing. “[Student employment] did weigh into our decision […] but it wasn’t a reason to keep it open,” said the director. 

Alex Marron ’27, Union Board President, said she was told about the decision this summer, but she is not concerned. “I think the main draw of Live Thursday is that people come to support their friends, it’s not the alcohol,” Marron said. 

However, for some students, the bar’s closure is upsetting. Upon finding out, Zach Mordan ’27 was surprised. “What the heck, I’m devastated […] I’m horrified, devastated and sober.” 

The surprise mainly comes from students not being formally told. There was no correspondence between students not on Union Board and Student Activities. “I don’t know why they didn’t tell students,” Marron said.

item.title: From Russia to Davidson: Living in exile
item.dc:creator: Staff
item.description: Visiting professor Elena Kostyuchenko and I meet at Summit on Main Street. She sits in the corner near the front window, watching two women take photos of each other with their lattes a few seats away. We talk about her Contemporary Reportage class, which I’m enrolled in, and The Davidsonian for a couple of minutes....
item.content:encoded:
Visiting professor Elena Kostyuchenko and I meet at Summit on Main Street. She sits in the corner near the front window, watching two women take photos of each other with their lattes a few seats away. 

We talk about her Contemporary Reportage class, which I’m enrolled in, and The Davidsonian for a couple of minutes. It’s an intimidating conversation; the whole time it feels like I’m a med student about to perform surgery on a world-renowned surgeon. 

Kostyuchenko left her homeland, Russia, on Feb. 24, 2022. It was the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

“I went to … report on the full-scale invasion [in Ukraine] because back then I was, like, the most experienced war correspondent in my newspaper,” she said. 

Kostyuchenko’s newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, has since ceased operations. The publication received official warnings about its war coverage from Russian state media regulators in March 2022, and was stripped of its media license in September of the same year. This month, Russia’s Ministry of Justice designated the news outlet as a “foreign agent.” 

Novaya Gazeta is one of many publications the Russian government cracked down on following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, claiming that they were spreading “false information” about the war. 

Kostyuchenko left for Ukraine assuming it would be temporary. But while she was away, Russian legislation changed. “They got two new articles into our criminal code. One of them called ‘deliberate dissemination of false information on the use of Russian armed forces,’” Kostyuchenko said. 

“It meant that any information which contradicts the official information of our ministry’s defense is a crime, and can be punished [with] up to 15 years in prison.” 

Worried for her and her associates’ safety, Novaya Gazeta asked Kostyuchenko to stay abroad for a while. Still, Kostyuchenko thought it was temporary. “I never meant to leave Russia. I never wanted to.” 

Kostyuchenko wrote four stories while in Ukraine. She travelled to Lviv, Odessa, Mykolaiv and Kherson. Mykolaiv was halfway surrounded by Russian forces at the time; Kherson was completely occupied. 

“I was able to cross the front line … and did some investigation there, and I was able to locate secret prisons there,” Kostyuchenko said of Kherson. “Russian soldiers and secret services would put kidnapped Ukrainians [there] and torture them and kill some of them. I was able to identify 44 people who were in this secret prison.” 

While Kostyuchenko was in Ukraine, her wife stayed in Russia to look after Kostyuchenko’s mother and take care of her affairs in case she was killed in Ukraine. “If it happen[ed], she shall be the one who could, you know, obtain [my] body, organize transfer of the body from Ukraine to Russia,” Kostyuchenko said. 

She delivered this information calmly. Kostyuchenko has been a war reporter for years – the possibility of dying on the field was not new to her. 

“Novaya Gazeta, while I was working there, four journalists were murdered,” she said. “They were all my colleagues. Some of my close friends outside of Novaya Gazeta were murdered, too.” 

A little over a month after arriving in Ukraine, Kostyuchenko was told by her editor-in-chief she was being targeted by Russian police and checkpoint agents had orders to shoot her on sight. She had to leave. 

Kostyuchenko spent the following months bouncing around Germany on various writing residencies. First Hamburg, then Munich and Berlin. In Berlin, she started working for Meduza, a Russian news organization operating in exile. 

“My first trip [with Meduza] was supposed to be in Iran, but before I took the plane to Iran, my chief editor asked me to obtain a Ukrainian visa, so after Iran I would travel back to Ukraine,” Kostyuchenko said. 

She travelled to Munich to begin the visa process. It was on the train ride back that, in Kostyuchenko’s words, “shit hit the fan.” 

“I realized that I had a severe headache and it’s getting higher and higher, and I thought I got COVID,” Kostyuchenko said. 

It was not COVID. After days of increasing sickness, multiple hospital visits and countless testing, German doctors told Kostyuchenko that she may have been poisoned. 

“And I started to laugh, honestly, because like … it felt so ridiculous. Like yeah, like a movie or something.” 

An investigation into the possible poisoning is still ongoing today. 

After recovering, Kostyuchenko finally got a Ukrainian permit and travelled back to the country. This time was different than the first. “I was like the only Russian journalist in Ukraine, and I had enormous attention from Ukrainian Secret Service. They were literally following me everywhere. My driver would report to them, and they were able to learn about every person I was meeting with.” 

The heightened scrutiny meant Kostyuchenko could not publish any stories without endangering her sources. 

Still, Kostyuchenko planned to continue working. It was her wife, who joined Kostyuchenko in Germany after she left Ukraine for the first time, that convinced her to leave Europe for the US. 

“At Novaya Gazeta, we kind of learn how to work under the pressure … but my wife didn’t have this experience, and she said she ended up with me in the middle of this crazy spy movie. It was so stressful for her,” Kostyuchenko said. “She was constantly on edge.” 

Alongside her reporting, Kostyuchenko was writing her debut book “Russia: Reporting from a Lost Country.” Dartmouth invited her to campus for a book tour in 2023 and ended up offering her a semester position. Primarily for her wife’s sake, Kostyuchenko took it. 

“And yeah, since that time, I’m in academia,” Kostyuchenko said. 

The transition from on-field reporting to teaching classrooms of students was a big one, but Kostyuchenko viewed it as a way to contribute to journalism despite the target on her back. 

“All my life I did pretty much the same thing. I was writing about Russia for Russians in the Russian language, and if I could continue that, I’d do it until I die. But now it’s kind of obvious. I cannot go to Russia and report.”

“But there are still journalists or people who form journalistic work now in Russia who can kind of do what I cannot, and I can help them, and that’s how I started my teaching. It’s not like I only started teaching once I got to the United States,” Kostyuchenko said. 

Kostyuchenko has taken on many Russian mentees, some as young as 16 years old. “Like if you do metaphors, we imagine journalism as a flame. And sometimes it’s high up in the sky, very bright. But sometimes it’s just, you know, a little candle, and you need to pass the candle to the next person through like wind and rain. So what I’m doing is like passing the candle.” 

Her Russian students and American students are working under fairly different circumstances, but Kostyuchenko said she sees common themes among both. “Of course, many [American] students are feeling anxiety and fear and uncertainty … The more I teach here, the more American students start to, you know, look around and get stuff out of current reality.” 

Davidson recently offered Kostyuchenko the opportunity to teach for another semester. Right now she teaches Contemporary Reportage and Literature of Catastrophe: Writing Lab, but looks to make some changes for the second half of the year. 

“I’m thinking about the journalism, what I have to offer, and I’m thinking between two classes. One of them would be investigative reporting and the other one would be war reporting,” Kostyuchenko said. “And I have a feeling that you guys need them both.”
